extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal scholars, and readers interested in English constitutional law and public finance
extracted.subtask_description: A legal-treatise style survey of the king's revenue (customs, excise, stamps, post-office, etc.), the nature and consequences of the national debt and sinking fund, and the effect of fiscal arrangements on the prerogative and balance of power between crown and parliament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidence of early import taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: The earlier any tax is laid on a commodity, the heavier it falls upon the consumer in the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained by the successive profits of intermediaries: the merchant charges profit on the duty advanced at importation; the stationer/printer/bookseller each charge profit on the whole sum they have advanced (including the duty), so the ultimate consumer pays the original duty plus the compounded profits of intermediaries. This principle applies particularly to imported manufactured or complicated goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excise duties as the most economical mode of taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: The excise duty...is doubtless, impartially speaking, the most oeconomical way of taxing the subject: the charges of levying, collecting, and managing the excise duties being considerably less in proportion, than in any other branch of the revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excises are often paid at a later stage (on consumption or retail sale), making the commodity cheaper to the consumer than an equivalent customs charge. Administrative costs are lower. Historical examples of excise application to beer, ale, cyder, perry, spirits, paper, malt, hops, candles, soap, etc., are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excise enforcement implicates liberty concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: The rigour and arbitrary proceedings of excise-laws seem hardly compatible with the temper of a free nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of fraud risks, excise officers often require power to enter and search houses at any hour and summary proceedings (conviction in two days by commissioners or justices without jury). This trade-off between efficient revenue collection and individual liberties is emphasized, with historical unpopularity cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salt duty as a distinct excise-like revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty upon salt is another distinct branch ... consists in an excise of 3s. 4d. per bushel imposed upon all salt; commissioners of the salt duties have by statute the same powers as those of other excises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not always called an excise because of different commissioners, the salt duty operates under similar powers and regulations and was made perpetual by statute 26 Geo. II c. 3. Intended as a concrete example of an excise-type branch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-office as mutually beneficial public revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: The post-office, or duty for the carriage of letters, is a manifest advantage to the public: the government acquires a large revenue; and the people do their business with greater ease, expedition, and cheapness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: History: originated with Parliament in 1642–49, organized regular weekly conveyance, saved public cost of postmasters. Exclusive rights to carriage are necessary to sustain the office; statutes and regulations later refined rates and penalties. Franking abuses and legislative fixes are discussed. Presented as an example where a revenue mechanism simultaneously serves public utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stamp duties authenticate instruments and deter forgery
rubrics_metrics.description: Stamp duties are a tax imposed upon all parchment and paper whereon any legal proceedings or private instruments are written... rising gradually from a penny to ten pounds. They authenticate instruments, and render it much more difficult than formerly to forge deeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts with taxing the contract itself (as in France), which engenders disputes about taxable nature of contracts. The English method (taxing the instrument) is argued to consult the ease of the subject and serve the state's purposes better. Historical origin: statute 5 & 6 W. & M. c. 21; amounts have since been increased.

rubrics_metrics.name: House and window taxes vs. privacy and inspection powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Duties upon houses and windows (hearth-money, house-tax, window-tax) have historically required inspection powers, sometimes even interior viewings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hearth-money (fumage/fuage) dates to Domesday; parliamentary statutes required local appointees to view the inside of houses annually. Hearth-money was abolished as oppressive and then replaced (with a house/window tax) which allowed surveyors to inspect house exteriors and to pass through houses two days a year to inspect windows. The entry/search element again raises civil liberty concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hackney coach and chair licences as localized beneficial revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: Duties arising from licences to hackney coaches and chairs form a branch of revenue governed by commissioners; the revenue is in truth a benefit to the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically limited numbers of licences were issued and the revenue applied (e.g., to street repairs). The tax's expense is felt by no single individual and licensing enables regulation of a refractory trade, argued as socially beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty on offices and pensions (1s. in the pound)
rubrics_metrics.description: A duty consisting in a payment of 1s. in the pound out of all salaries, fees, and perquisites of offices and pensions payable by the crown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imposed by statute 31 Geo. II c. 22 and administered under commissioners of the land tax. Characterized as a highly popular taxation; part of the king's perpetual extraordinary revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: National debt: borrowing to anticipate future revenues and creation of funds
rubrics_metrics.description: The policy to anticipate the revenues of posterity by borrowing immense sums for the current service of the state and to lay no more taxes than would suffice to pay the annual interest of the sums so borrowed — thereby converting the principal debt into a new species of property, transferrable at any time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tracing origins to Florence (A.D. 1344). The capital of the national debt (funded and unfunded) had grown very large (example figure Jan 1765 > £145,000,000). Interest and management charges consume large annual sums; revenues are mortgaged to pay interest; this gives rise to funds (aggregate, general, south sea). Explanation of how borrowing produces transferrable securities and affects circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public creditor's property is a portion of national taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: The property of a creditor of the publick consists in a certain portion of the national taxes: by how much therefore he is the richer, by so much the nation, which pays these taxes, is the poorer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained via example: if A's income is £100 and pays £50 interest to B, half of A's property's value is transferred to creditor B. The creditor's property exists as a demand upon the debtor (the state/taxes). This frames public debt as transferring real economic value from taxpayers to creditors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages of public debt (circulation and liquidity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The only advantage that can result to a nation from public debts is the increase of circulation by multiplying the cash of the kingdom, creating a new species of money always ready to be employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debt creates transferable securities productive of profit even when idle; a certain proportion of debt is useful to a trading people, though the 'proper' proportion is not specified by the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disadvantages of excessive national debt
rubrics_metrics.description: Large national incumbrances far exceed commercial benefit and are productive of the greatest inconveniences: they hurt trade, may drain specie to foreigners, support idle creditors at expense of industrious taxpayers, and weaken the state's defensive resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four specific harms are listed: (1) enormous taxes on necessities raise costs and hurt trade/manufactures; (2) if debt is owed to foreigners they draw specie out or demand privileges; (3) if owed to domestic subjects it charges active taxpayers to support idle creditors; (4) it anticipates resources needed for national defense. Interest paid could otherwise maintain a war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation of separate funds and the sinking fund principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate funds (produce of specific taxes) were united into aggregate and general funds and a south sea fund; surplusses are directed by statute to the sinking fund to sink and lower the national debt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Union of funds made them mutual securities; surpluses beyond interest are carried to a sinking fund (statute 3 Geo. I c. 7). Prudent application of sinking-fund sums is of utmost importance; example: prudent application enabled reduction of over two million sterling of public debt in 1765.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil list: purpose, settlement, and fiscal consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The civil list is properly the whole of the king's revenue in his own distinct capacity; it defrays all expenses relating to civil government (household, salaries, ambassadors, maintenance of royal family, privy purse, secret service, pensions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern settlement: the king accepted a limited sum (£800,000 per annum) charged on the aggregate fund; hereditary revenues were carried into the aggregate fund. The civil list's liquidation together with interest on national debt and sinking-fund produce constitutes the perpetual tax produce. Debate: though some complain of its increase, the author argues the modern civil list is better for crown and people given certainty and relinquishment of feudal burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiscal centralization empowers the executive
rubrics_metrics.description: The collection and management of vast revenue, being placed in the hands of the crown, have given rise to a multitude of new officers, created by and removable at the royal pleasure, which extend the influence of government throughout the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists examples: customs commissioners and dependents in every port; commissioners of excise and subalterns inland; postmasters and servants on roads; commissioners of stamps and distributors; officers of salt duty; surveyors of houses and windows; receivers of land tax; managers of lotteries; commissioners of hackney coaches. These officers' dependence on the crown gives the executive extensive influence. This is presented as a natural consequence of large revenues and central management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal reforms have curtailed formerly extensive prerogative
rubrics_metrics.description: Many laws for ascertaining, limiting, and restraining the crown's prerogative have been made within little more than a century past (e.g., Petition of Right, abolition of star chamber, habeas corpus, Bill of Rights, Act of Settlement, triennial/septennial parliaments, judicial independence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes that these reforms appear to have greatly curtailed the crown's powers since James I; yet also observes that customary additions to the hereditary revenue at accession (and parliamentary settlements like the civil list) restore to each prince a degree of constitutional independence. Thus there is a tension between statutory curbs and fiscal/constitutional practices that preserve royal influence.
